articles.title: China's new challenge as natural disasters strike - fake AI videos
articles.summary: Storms and flooding incidents over the last few months have seen fake videos inundating social media.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Chinese state media Image caption, 
Screenshot shows Chinese state media debunking AI content By Stephen McDonell 
China correspondent 
- Published 6 hours ago 
As China deals with the fallout of Typhoon Noul that made landfall over the weekend, officials will be painfully aware that they will likely have an additional challenge to deal with: dangerously misleading videos created with Artificial Intelligence (AI). 
Powerful storms and flooding incidents over the last few months have seen fake videos inundating social media platforms – these include images of dead bodies floating in floodwaters, the false depiction of severe flooding in areas actually not affected and others with blatantly fake details of emergency response efforts. 
In some areas, videos containing false information about power outages prompted residents to panic buy emergency supplies. 
Other videos capitalise on real-life incidents. 
Flooding in Hengzhou city, Guangxi in early July caused hundreds of snakes to escape from a breeding farm. Then fake images were also published showing crocodiles being released into a river. 
In an already tense and dangerous situation involving mass evacuations and complex rescue operations, authorities want to avoid panic. Now they fear that AI technology - which China is pouring billions of dollars into - is providing simple, accessible tools that can be used to trick the public. 
"Many of these content creators use disaster news to try to gain followers, knowing that more sensational or exaggerated content will garner more likes and more views. They are deliberately fabricating information to grab people's attention," Huang Zhihua, Deputy Chief in charge of online public security for Zhejiang Police Department told Chinese state media. 
In recent weeks, there have been arrests and punishment – ranging from detention awaiting criminal prosecution to fines – for the creation of bogus reports and video content. 
But experts are warning that an unprecedented crisis of misinformation could be looming. 
Image source, Social media Image caption, 
Fake content purportedly shows crocodiles being released into a river 
In an article published by the newspaper of the Communist Party's Central Party School, Professor Chen Bin said, "AI dramatically lowers the technical barriers to producing false information. Individuals no longer require sophisticated technical skills. By simply prompting AI tools, they can rapidly generate convincing text, images, audio and video… which is highly realistic but entirely fabricated content, manufactured on a large scale." 
Professor Gao Fuping, from the East China University of Political Science and Law, told the BBC that motivation for the publishing of such false content ranges from those who do it "to create something amusing without thinking about the consequences", to those who want to "generate traffic for personal gain" or those who wish to deliberately "cause panic or social unrest". 
"Some users think the online world is anonymous and unregulated or that they cannot be traced," he said. 
There have been calls for all AI-generated content to be clearly stamped but other users can then just re-edit the material removing the markings. 
Professor Xu Xiaoke from Beijing Normal University told the BBC that greater efforts were also needed to verify geographic locations with timestamps and the checking of image sources. 
"That said, I would also stress that detection technology still lags behind generation technology. We're in a constant cat-and-mouse game. So we should not assume that technology alone can identify AI-generated content with the click of a button," he warned. 
Image source, Social media Image caption, 
AI content purports to show the rescue of pigs prioritised over people 
The Chinese government is embracing AI in its bid to become the leading tech superpower. 
In 2017, it announced that AI would be "the main driving force" of the country's progress. 
Vast sums of money is pouring into AI businesses seeking more capital, fuelling domestic competition. The state-controlled wire service Xinhua reports that the country has over 6,000 "AI companies". 
In this climate, Prof Xu believes that China needs to build "trusted information infrastructure". This could include official government early warning systems and disaster interfaces which news organisations can access. 
But there have been instances of official sources, including government-controlled media, deliberately downplaying disasters, which has led to some public mistrust in this area. 
Earlier in July, local journalists were asked to "soften" their language to describe a major breach in the wall of the Liulan Dam near Naning as an "opening" or "gap". 
Officials appeared to be trying to make the breach sound less alarming but the consequences were deadly. Water bursting through the broken dam led to at least 26 deaths downstream. 
Figure caption, 
Fatal Typhoon Maysak floods burst dam wall in China 
And this is not an isolated incident. 
In 2021, local officials were arrested, accused of concealing or underreporting 139 deaths in Henan province. 
Incidents like these have resulted in a trust vacuum that has made it much easier for bad actors to spread fake content. 
But police are imploring people to trust accredited sources during emergencies. 
"When encountering disaster-related information from an unknown source, approach it with scepticism and rely on official announcements," Gao Kai from the Ningbo Public Security Bureau said. 
He also tried to reassure the public that the creators of false information would be caught, saying that "the internet is not a lawless zone. Public security authorities will continue to intensify efforts to crack down on illegal online activity". 
"We've created a specialised task force to monitor social media closely, especially short video platforms. They will investigate and handle these cases quickly, cracking down in a very strict manner". 
Punishment could range from a fine to up to seven years in prison if the fallout of the misinformation is serious enough. 
On 23 July, China's Cyberspace Administration also announced a nationwide crackdown on fake internet content related to floods and other disasters, ordering its local branches to focus on catching out fabricated data, malicious editing, staged scenes, misattributed historical events and those impersonating officials. In addition, it called on social media platforms to strengthen the review of the content they are publishing. 
Prof Gao believes "the answer is public education combined with law enforcement", saying that there was a "need to publicise real cases where people have been punished." 
He added that "the harm caused by AI-generated fake content is ultimately the result of how people choose to use the technology - not the technology itself", adding that existing laws were sufficient to deal with it. 
However, others are not so confident. Professor Chen pointed out that "AI technology continues to evolve much faster than legal frameworks. As new legal questions emerge, AI misinformation remains a considerable challenge." 
Shanghai and Washington based lawyer Peter Pang says lawyers around the world are seeing an explosion in the number of cases dealing with these issues. 
He believes that the companies that create AI apps and the platforms used to publish fake videos and other material must be held legally accountable along with the people who create misinformation. 
"The first line would be the platforms, because they're the ones that are the enablers. They're the ones that allow this to go out," he told the BBC. 
He used a hypothetical example of a person who runs over a pedestrian following panic induced by a fake post on social media. 
"The video creator might say 'you ran over somebody. That's your problem. I didn't do it.' But let's think it through. You created the foundation from which people reacted. If you created that panic, you need to have responsibility for consequences that occur." 
And Professor Xu warns that "AI-generated misinformation is likely to increase not only in volume but in the speed with which it spreads." 
"Looking ahead, political elections, public health emergencies, armed conflicts, natural disasters and issues affecting people's livelihoods are all likely to become high-risk areas for AI-generated misinformation. 
"Instead of waiting for false information to go viral before trying to contain it, governments and platforms should now be preparing in advance."

articles.title: Chinese chipmaker shares surge nearly 470% in blockbuster stock market debut
articles.summary: The company's shares soared by nearly 470% in its market debut, as the AI boom drives chip demand.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Reuters By Peter Hoskins Business reporter 
- Published 27 July 2026 
Shares in China's biggest memory chip maker have soared by nearly 470% as they made their debut on the Shanghai Stock Exchange's tech-heavy Star Market. 
The surge has pushed ChangXin Memory Technologies' (CXMT) stock market valuation to around 3.3 trillion yuan ($487bn; £365bn), making it the most valuable listed company in mainland China. 
The spectacular debut comes despite a sharp sell-off in technology stocks around the world this month. 
CXMT manufactures dynamic random-access memory (Dram) chips that power AI data centres, mobile phones, PCs, tablets and other devices. 
The firm, which was founded in 2016 by Chairman Zhu Yiming, is headquartered in Hefei, Anhui Province in eastern China. 
The company has said it plans to use most of the proceeds from the initial public offering (IPO) to boost production of memory chips and carry out more research and developments. 
The stellar performance of its IPO will offer some comfort to Chinese financial officials, who have been rolling out measures to help curb a stock market slump that wiped out more than $1.5tn in recent weeks. 
Analysts said the jump was also being driven by demand for the shares far outstripping supply. 
"The reason for the extraordinary bounce this morning is that only 7% of the shares are available for trading," Anna Macdonald, investment strategy director at Hargreaves Lansdown told the BBC's Today programme. 
It also highlights Chinese investors' strong appetite for a homegrown chipmaker, as the government in Beijing pushes ahead with plans to make its technology industry self-reliant. 
South Korean tech giants Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix and US-based Micron dominate the Dram market, with the three companies accounting for around 90% of global production. 
Earlier this month, SK Hynix raised $26.5bn (£19.8bn) in its New York share offering , marking the largest ever listing by a foreign firm in the US. 
The company, a key supplier to AI chip giant Nvidia, said it had sold 177.9 million American depositary shares for $149 each. 
The shares surged as much as 17% in their first day of trading on the Nasdaq but have since given up some of that gain. 
SK Hynix saw its market value top $1tn in its home country in May, lifted by the boom in demand for AI chips. 
Once an affordable component used to build devices, memory prices have more than doubled in recent months - and are still rising. 
Some big tech firms have hiked the price of popular gadgets, such as tablets and video game consoles , to cope with rising component costs. 
Ellie Wong, an analyst at technology research firm TrendForce, told Reuters , external such price increases were expected to continue until the end of 2027. 
"Amid persistent supply shortages, many customers are seeking to diversify their memory supplier base, which should significantly benefit CXMT and create more business opportunities," she said.

articles.title: Shein swings to $99m loss as Trump tariffs hit sales
articles.summary: The announcement comes as the fast fashion giant prepares for its stock market debut in Hong Kong.
articles.full_text:
Image source, In Pictures via Getty Images By Peter Hoskins Business reporter 
- Published 27 July 2026 
Shein says it swung to a quarterly loss as its sales slowed after US President Donald Trump removed an import duty exemption on small packages. 
It also comes as uncertainty remains over the tit-for-tat US-China tariffs wars, which is currently paused. 
The fast-fashion giant, which has its headquarters in Singapore but was founded in China, said it lost $99m (£74.1m) in the first three months of the year, compared with a net income of $395m a year earlier. 
The announcement is part of the firm's preparations ahead of its stock market debut in Hong Kong, although the filing did not give any details on the size, timetable or pricing of the planned initial public offering (IPO). 
"In response to the increased duties and taxes, we are pursuing a wide range of options, including increasing our prices in the US market to offset a portion of the increased costs," Shein said in the filing. 
The company also said the Iran war had hit demand, increased costs and caused delays of deliveries in some markets. 
The first-quarter figures also partly reflected a paper loss of $328m due to an accounting change for special investor shares. The shares can be turned into ordinary stock later, and their value can change before a listing. 
The filing showed that in the year to the end of March 2026 Shein had 281 million active customers - a rise of more than 16% on a year earlier - who placed a total of more than one billion orders. 
On 10 July, the China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC) gave Shein approval for a Hong Kong share sale after failed attempts to list in New York and London. 
The Hong Kong share listing is expected to take place in the coming months. 
The figures show the impact of a Trump-signed executive order to end a global tariff exemption that had been used by US shoppers of low-cost goods. 
That order, which came into effect on 29 August 2025, broadened an earlier presidential action which specifically targeted cheap products from China and Hong Kong to cover the rest of the world. 
The so-called de minimis exemption had allowed goods valued at $800 or less to enter the US without paying any tariffs. US consumers relied on the exemption to buy cheap goods from online commerce sites like Shein and Temu. 
The White House said the global exemption was being used to "evade tariffs and funnel deadly synthetic opioids" to the US. 
"The removal of the US de minimis exemption has had an adverse impact on our sales in the US and the overall growth of our net revenues," Shein said in the filing. 
Earlier in July, the European Union imposed a €3 (£2.56; $3.42) levy on low-value e-commerce imports. 
The measure is aimed to curb what the trading bloc has said is unfair competition from China.

articles.title: Watch: Scaffolding tumbles from Hong Kong building as Typhoon Noul makes landfall
articles.summary: Typhoon Noul is the strongest to make landfall in China so far this year, according to state media.
articles.full_text:
Watch: Scaffolding tumbles from Hong Kong building as Typhoon Noul makes landfall
Watch: Scaffolding tumbles from Hong Kong building as Typhoon Noul makes landfall 
Close 
Police said they received numerous calls after multi-storey scaffolding along Cheung Sha Wan Road collapsed in powerful winds on Saturday. No injuries have been reported. 
Typhoon Noul made landfall in southern China on Sunday morning, lashing the region with strong winds and heavy rain and forcing Hong Kong airport to cancel around 360 passenger flights. 
The typhoon is the strongest to make landfall in China in 2026 to date, according to state media.

articles.title: ‘We have lost everything’: extreme rainfall across Asia brings flash floods and typhoons
articles.summary: From Afghanistan to Taiwan, unprecedented deluge highlights devastating impact of climate breakdown“It rained for 10 days and 10 nights, non-stop – I’d never seen anything like it,” says Anar Gul, a construction worker who lives in the remote district of Dur Baba in eastern Afghanistan.The houses in his village are built from stone and mud, which makes them extremely vulnerable to heavy rains. After days of rain, Gul’s kitchen collapsed and his neighbour, Sayed Afsar Sadat, saw a large part of his house completely destroyed. “Rains like this are coming heavier and earlier each year,” says Sadat. “They are destroying the roads and washing away our crops. It’s impacting us directly.” Continue reading...
articles.full_text:
Bangladesh is one of several countries in the region to experience heavy rains and flash floods. Photograph: Rayhan Ahmed/Zuma Press Wire/Shutterstock 
From Afghanistan to Taiwan, unprecedented deluge highlights devastating impact of climate breakdown By Natasha May and Jonathan Watts 
“It rained for 10 days and 10 nights, non-stop – I’d never seen anything like it,” says Anar Gul, a construction worker who lives in the remote district of Dur Baba in eastern Afghanistan . 
The houses in his village are built from stone and mud, which makes them extremely vulnerable to heavy rains. After days of rain, Gul’s kitchen collapsed and his neighbour, Sayed Afsar Sadat, saw a large part of his house completely destroyed. “Rains like this are coming heavier and earlier each year,” says Sadat. “They are destroying the roads and washing away our crops. It’s impacting us directly.” 
View image in fullscreen 
Anar Gul, who lives in a remote mountain village in the Dur Baba district of eastern Afghanistan, says he has never seen rain like it. Photograph: IFRC/Mark South. 
Last week, torrential rains and flash floods wiped out villages and towns in Afghanistan, leaving at least 31 people dead and hundreds missing. It’s been a similar picture in neighbouring countries, with the monsoon rains sparking chaos across the region. India, Bangladesh and Pakistan have all seen erratic, sudden heavy dumps of water. 
Jesmin Akter lived in the city of Chattogram, on the south-eastern coast of Bangladesh, which received a record 412.3mm of rainfall in 24 hours in early July, leading to the flash flood that swept through the Banshkhali district where they live. She says her children “understand that we are in a very bad situation”. 
Overnight the rains took the little they had; their poultry died, their paddy field flooded, their house collapsed and all their belongings in it – children’s books, school bags, toys, clothes, kitchen items – ruined. 
Akter carried her six children through chest-deep water to her mother’s house. There they stayed in the crowded conditions for over a week until the water receded. 
View image in fullscreen 
Residents and rescue workers inspect buildings damaged by heavy flooding in the eastern province of Nuristan, Afghanistan. Photograph: Wahidullah Kakar/AP 
“We have lost everything,” Akter said. Their house beside the canal was not in a good condition, but a few months ago the family had repaired it. “Now the flood has destroyed it again. We have no money. We are surviving on the food assistance we receive from different organisations.” They have gone back to the ruins of their home, but her children sleep on plastic sheets laid on the wet floor and she worries for their safety, especially that the unsanitary conditions will lead to disease. Her daughter has developed a fever. 
As wildfires rage across Europe and North America, the unprecedented rains continue elsewhere. While South Korea swings between heatwave and downpour, in Japan and Vietnam torrential rain has led to landslides . China, meanwhile, has seen bouts of extreme rainfall since the flood season began in April, according to the water resources ministry in mid-July, marking the start of a month-long peak flood control window. More than 600 rivers have since risen above warning levels – a 35% jump from the average for the same period over the past five years. 
View image in fullscreen 
Sayed Afsar Sadat in Dur Baba says rains are destroying the roads and washing away crops. Photograph: IFRC/Meer Abdullah Rasikh. 
In the south-western city of Chongqing, a huge landslide after torrential rain killed at least 11 people and left 50 missing, with rescue efforts still ongoing. Separately, a flash flood at a scenic camping spot in the north-central province of Gansu left 10 people dead and injured 23 others. 
The flood season across the region has been exacerbated by successive storms. Typhoon Noul, the strongest to make landfall in China so far this year, prompted the evacuation of more than 890,000 people in Guangdong as of Sunday evening, according to provincial authorities. In early July, Typhoon Maysak inundated parts of Guangxi and swept through commercial snake farms , allowing hundreds of snakes to escape. 
Forecasters have warned that more wet weather is on the way. Much of northern China, including Beijing, is expected to receive 20% to 50% more rain than usual, while four to six typhoons are forecast to make landfall in or affect the country this summer, above the average of 4.2, according to the China Meteorological Administration . 
Taiwan, an island that lies in the path of typhoons in the north-west Pacific, has also seen a rise in extreme rainfall. In June, repeated downpours caused more than NT$330m (about US$10.2m) in agricultural losses across Taiwan, according to the agriculture ministry , while the capital Taipei recorded its highest monthly rainfall in more than a century. 
View image in fullscreen 
Torrential rain flooded the streets of Dhaka in Bangladesh. Photograph: Mohammad Ponir Hossain/Reuters 
The extreme weather across the region can clearly be linked to climate change. Climate scientists have long predicted that large areas of Asia will disproportionately suffer from more intense heat, humidity and drought as a result of climate disruption caused by the burning of gas, oil and coal. The most recent report by the United Nations’ Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change said rising temperatures raise the threat of “floods in monsoon regions in south, south-east and east Asia, and glacier melting in the Hindu Kush Himalaya region”. skip past newsletter promotion 
after newsletter promotion 
And World Weather Attribution scientists have warned that extreme rainfall from cyclones is being “supercharged” in south-east Asia, with a clear pattern of increasingly heavy rain over recent decades. 
View image in fullscreen 
In early July, Typhoon Maysak inundated parts of Guangxi in south China. Photograph: Cao Yiming/Xinhua/AP 
The year 2025 saw devastating storms and rainfall across the region. It also saw ocean temperatures rise to record heights. So far, this year has brought record-breaking heatwaves . Extreme rainfall is more common and more intense because of human-caused climate breakdown across most of the world, particularly in Europe , most of Asia, central and eastern North America, and parts of South America, Africa and Australia. This is because warmer air can hold more water vapour and flooding has most likely become more frequent and severe in these locations as a result. 
“More intense rainfall is an expected consequence of us heating the planet by burning fossil fuels and building up more carbon dioxide in the atmosphere. A warmer atmosphere can carry more water, so when it rains, it rains harder. Also hotter conditions cause air to rise faster and drive more intense thunderstorms,” said Richard Betts, head of the climate impacts strategic area at the Met Office Hadley Centre. 
The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC) in providing aid helped the Guardian obtain interviews with those affected. 
View image in fullscreen 
Typhoon Noul (pictured in Hong Kong) prompted the evacuation of more than 890,000 people in Guangdong. Photograph: Venron Yuen/Nexpher/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock 
Dr Hosam Faysal, the head of IFRC’s country delegation in Afghanistan, said “these are the very real, humanitarian effects of a changing climate … becoming increasingly volatile”. 
Faysal urged governments to ensure there was more investment in locally-led preparedness and mitigation in order to reduce the loss of life and suffering before climate-related disasters happened. 
“The coming forecast El Niño is a clear example – waiting to respond to the extreme needs we can see coming only once they arrive will cost lives.” 
- 
Research by Yu-chen Li

articles.summary: Four decades after he and George Michael became the first western pop act to tour the country, Ridgeley recalls silent gigs, awkward embassy receptions – and the ‘bloody ludicrous’ hiring of Lindsay Anderson as directorWham! special – read about George Michael’s great lost superstar duets albumThere has always been something surreal about Wham!’s 1985 trip to China. Continue reading...
articles.full_text:
‘I think it counts as a historical event’… Wham! visit Tiananmen Square, 7 April, 1985. Photograph: Pat Benic/Reuters 
View image in fullscreen 
‘I think it counts as a historical event’… Wham! visit Tiananmen Square, 7 April, 1985. Photograph: Pat Benic/Reuters 
‘I thought it didn’t stand a cat’s chance in hell’: Andrew Ridgeley on Wham’s surreal trip to China
Four decades after he and George Michael became the first western pop act to tour the country, Ridgeley recalls silent gigs, awkward embassy receptions – and the ‘bloody ludicrous’ hiring of Lindsay Anderson as director 
- 
Wham! special – read about George Michael’s great lost superstar duets album 
T here has always been something surreal about Wham!’s 1985 trip to China. George Michael and Andrew Ridgeley looked like alien visitors on the streets of Beijing, their bouffant hair and flamboyant outfits setting them apart from the Mao jackets and drab uniforms of the Chinese people they encountered. 
View image in fullscreen 
Andrew Ridgeley attends the screening of Wham! 10 Days in China in London. Photograph: Ian West/PA 
Now the full strangeness of the duo’s brief trip, which made them the first western pop act to play in the country, is explored in a fascinating documentary film, Wham! 10 Days in China . Using previously unseen archive footage and featuring new interviews with many of the people involved in the tour, it shows the extraordinary impact Wham!’s two concerts had on their Chinese audience, as well as providing a snapshot of a country on the brink of great change. 
Yet for Michael and Ridgeley, the tour was less about expanding cultural horizons and more about hardheaded commercial logic: as masterminded by their manager, Simon Napier-Bell, it was designed to create such an international sensation that they would be catapulted to top-tier status in the US without having to undergo the slog of a 90-date arena tour that might have put Michael’s voice at risk. 
“And it worked,” says Ridgeley, now 63 and white-haired, looking athletic in a long-sleeved top and shorts – a kind of Club Tropicana smart casual – when we meet on a warm summer’s day in central London. 
“When the idea was originally proposed to George and myself, I thought it didn’t stand a cat’s chance in hell. I wasn’t a fan, but George was pretty immovable on not touring in the States to the extent to which we would have to. It was a bit of a Hobson’s choice – China or bust. Reluctantly, I agreed to it. But it did ultimately achieve our aim. We were on national news in the States, we were in the newspapers.” 
View image in fullscreen 
Excitement and confusion … a scene from Wham! 10 Days in China. Photograph: Martyn Goddard/© Andrew Ridgeley, Big Geoff Overseas, Robobuild t/a George Michael Entertainment 
The film shows Wham! performing their hits in Beijing and Guangzhou, as well as dealing with the many other demands placed on them – having to make polite speeches at a banquet with Chinese officials, for example. Michael clearly found it hard to put up with a reception at the British embassy – “that was just not something that he cared for at all: the formality, the small talk, the artificial nature of the meeting”, Ridgeley says – and later went missing after chatting awkwardly to fans at a shop. For his part, Ridgeley bridled at the demands of the press, who were there to provide the publicity the band needed: we see him refusing to take his sunglasses off at a photoshoot on the Great Wall and unable to contain his disdain for journalists at a press conference. 
“There was a fair bit of pressure, which wouldn’t have been there in usual circumstances – it was very different from a usual tour,” Ridgeley recalls. “We went there to achieve a goal, it was constructed to achieve a purpose, and so the context was very different.” He remembers having chaperones and feeling “slightly restricted” in Beijing. 
View image in fullscreen 
‘I thought the trip didn’t stand a cat’s chance in hell’ … Wham! in Beijing. Photograph: © Andrew Ridgeley, Big Geoff Overseas, Robobuild t/a George Michael Entertainment. Photograph by Martyn Goddard 
There was certainly a strange atmosphere at the Beijing concert: the audience, who had little idea of what to expect or how to react, had been told to stay in their seats, and the band walked out to silence; while some people did get up to dance, one man was taken away by the police for getting too exuberant. Even playing their song Freedom could have been construed as a political act. 
But for some Chinese fans, the tour provided revelatory exposure to western music. The film captures the excitement and confusion felt by Chinese audiences and includes interviews with musicians who were directly affected. “I think it counts as a historical event,” says Cheng Fangyuan, the singer who performed Chinese-language versions of Wham!’s songs on the tapes handed out to ticket holders. “It was like opening a window.” 
View image in fullscreen 
Wham in China. Photograph: Peter Charlesworth/LightRocket/Getty Images 
The reason there is so much original footage of the tour is because Wham!’s management had arranged for a documentary to be made about it. In one of the most peculiar hirings in film history, the man they chose to oversee the film was Lindsay Anderson , the high-minded director of This Sporting Life and O Lucky Man!, who was then 61 and at a low ebb in his career. 
The partnership proved to be an unhappy one: Anderson and Wham! did not take to each other, and the director was fired six months later, when the band rejected the film he presented to them. 
The story of this ill-starred collaboration is an important strand in the new film. Anderson’s name was first put forward by the producer Martin Lewis, while Wham!’s co-manager, Jazz Summers (who died in 2015), is widely thought to have played a key role in the hiring. 
“I thought it was bloody ludicrous,” says Ridgeley. “Someone like him, with his provenance and cinematic pedigree in the genre that he worked in, was just not the right fit for Wham! He only did it for the money – his letters on the subject make it very clear. He didn’t like us at all – he didn’t like Wham!, he didn’t like the idea of Wham!” 
To make matters worse, Anderson twisted his knee at the Great Wall, on only the second day of the trip, reducing his involvement in the shoot, which was largely left to his five cinematographers. 
Anderson himself appears on camera in footage used for the new film. Asked what it is he does, he replies, “Well, I’ve been wondering about that for the last couple of weeks. If anybody’s got any idea, I’d be happy to know.” 
There is an excruciatingly revealing moment later on when Anderson, walking with a stick, approaches Michael from behind and claps him on the shoulder, while the star is holding court; Michael very conspicuously fails to turn round to acknowledge him. 
Ridgeley remembers being appalled when he viewed Anderson’s cut. “It was as dull as dishwater and just not what we wanted as a record of the tour there, so it was just not fit for purpose,” he says. “It was a pretty straightforward and uncomplicated brief, to record Wham! in China. Lindsay evidently was extremely conflicted and would rather have made a film that Wham! weren’t in or wasn’t about Wham!” 
He tried watching Anderson’s cut again last year: “I couldn’t make it all the way through – it was so dull.” 
View image in fullscreen 
‘It is about trying to keep Wham! in the musical consciousness’ … present-day Ridgeley in the new film. Photograph: © Craig Hastings 
Wham! hired video director Andy Morahan to make a reworked version of Anderson’s film, which was given the title Wham! in China: Foreign Skies and shown to 72,000 fans at the band’s final concert at Wembley Stadium in June 1986. 
The raw footage that Anderson’s crew had shot lay in storage for decades. No one had reopened the 100-plus cans containing the original reels of Super 16 film until director Mike Christie started work in September 2024. He and his team discovered more than 20 hours of footage, although the reels had been extensively cut to stitch together Anderson’s film and Foreign Skies. 
They could not find the film copy of Anderson’s original documentary, and decided to use completely different footage to make the new film (some concert shots were borrowed from Foreign Skies). 
Anderson kept a taped copy of his rejected cut, entitled If You Were There …, which is held in his archives at the University of Stirling. Michael prevented the film from being shown publicly, although it could be viewed by researchers on appointment. Following Michael’s death in 2016, it was finally screened to an audience as part of the BFI’s 2024 Anderson season, with the blessing of Ridgeley and Michael’s estate. 
View image in fullscreen 
‘George was pretty immovable on not touring in the States’… footage was shot during the 1985 trip for an ill-fated documentary. Photograph: © Neal Preston 
But Anderson’s admirers will be disappointed to hear that any official release of the film remains unlikely. “It won’t happen because George was very much against it ever seeing the light of day,” Ridgeley says. “If it was down to me, I don’t think I would have any particular problem with it.” He once even mooted the idea of the three films that have now been made about the China tour being collected as a box set. 
Wham! 10 Days in China is the third documentary about the band in recent years, following Netflix’s Wham! (2023) and the BBC’s Wham!: Last Christmas Unwrapped (2024). The idea of looking back on the band’s legacy was a consequence of Michael’s untimely death, Ridgeley says. “Prior to that, George wasn’t going to be developing a Wham! legacy when he was pursuing his own career – that was understood by all.” 
Ridgeley hopes there can be further projects to keep Wham!’s music alive. “It’s about developing new audiences and it is about trying to keep Wham! there or thereabouts in the musical consciousness. Fortunately we’ve got a really great catalogue of songs that assist us in that. All good music transcends generations and Wham!’s is no exception.”

The collapse of the rules-based order is not confined to the land: we’re imperilled as centuries of maritime cooperation sink beneath the waves 
T he US military campaign to protect merchant shipping from Iranian attacks by asserting direct maritime control in the strait of Hormuz is not an idea unique to Donald Trump’s administration. Almost exactly 200 years ago, in the period 1825-27, a powerful US naval squadron led by Commodore John Rodgers was sent to the Mediterranean to defend American ships from the depredations of Greek corsairs and pirates. 
For all the new-minted republic’s brave talk of liberty, the US squadron did not assist Greece’s ongoing “regime change” struggle for independence from the Ottoman empire. Its sole, self-serving purpose was to defend US trade, markets and business interests. After abandoning his call for a people’s revolution in Tehran , this, too, is what Trump’s reckless war with Iran has now boiled down to. 
Although the US has not ratified the 1982 UN convention on the law of the sea, which establishes a legal right of freedom of passage without interference by littoral states, it has historically upheld the principle of freedom of navigation or mare liberum (the free sea) developed by Hugo Grotius, a 17th-century Dutch jurist. Rejecting Iran’s claims, Marco Rubio, US secretary of state, declared in June that “no country is allowed to charge tolls or fees on an international waterway”. 
Yet Trump has since suggested the US itself may yet do exactly that and impose tolls. Although he later rowed back , last month’s “ memorandum of understanding ” with Iran accepts that it has a right, with Oman, to monetise transit through the strait of Hormuz. Despite the resumption of US attacks and Trump’s increasingly hysterical threats , the MOU currently remains the only basis for a future peace deal. 
Two-faced Trump’s equivocal stance reflects a wider breakdown in the “free sea” consensus underpinning maritime law – and hastens the overall degradation of the international rules-based order. Trump believes nation states (or at least the US) have an absolute right to act unilaterally in their own interests, unconstrained by laws, treaties or regard for the “ global commons ” of the high seas. 
The destabilising ramifications of this approach, emulated by other countries, grow clearer by the day . This new 21st-century war of the sea does not involve titanic clashes between Bismarck-class battleships or huge naval showdowns such as Jutland and Midway. But its frontlines are the same as ever: defence, security, borders, free trade, money, power. 
Today’s war of the sea has many aspects. One is the spreading impact of precedents set by the Hormuz standoff. In Yemen, Iran-aligned Houthi militias have begun a copycat blockade of the Bab al-Mandab strait, at the mouth of the Red Sea, in reprisal, they claim, for attacks by Saudi Arabia. Two oil tankers were struck this week , further spooking energy markets and presaging wider escalation. 
Also potentially fatal for international norms is the post-Hormuz debate in Indonesia about imposing tolls in the strait of Malacca , through which 22% of global maritime shipping passes. Might Turkey adopt the US-Iran approach and charge for passage through the Bosphorus? Or Spain in the strait of Gibraltar? The dire implications for global trade and supply chains are obvious. About 80% of goods traded worldwide by volume go by sea. 
Friction over seaborne trade aside, overt maritime clashes between regional rivals are increasing, particularly in the South China Sea and the waters around Taiwan. Expansionist China’s creation of artificial, militarised islands on obscure reefs and sporadic confrontations with neighbours such as the Philippines are the root cause. Like the US, Beijing rejects international law when it doesn’t suit it – notably the 2016 ruling by the permanent court of arbitration, which found its claim to sovereignty over most of the South China Sea lacked a legal basis . 
China crossed another red line last week when one of its missile destroyers undertook a live-fire drill inside Japan’s exclusive economic zone, about 180km (110 miles) from Okinotori, Japan’s southernmost island. Tokyo and Beijing have longstanding maritime disputes. But tensions rose sharply after Japan’s new prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, suggested a Chinese bid to seize Taiwan could trigger a Japanese military response. Few weeks go by without reports of Chinese air and sea exercises in preparation for a not-so-hypothetical amphibious assault on Taiwan. 
The fact a Russian frigate accompanied the offending Chinese warship off Japan points to another major actor in the global war of the sea. Vladimir Putin’s once-vaunted Black Sea fleet has suffered severe losses , caused by Ukraine’s missiles and drones, since 2022. Its ships no longer control the Black Sea, mostly cowering in port. As if to compensate, hybrid “grey zone” Russian military maritime operations against Ukraine’s European allies are expanding . Baltic undersea pipelines and communications cables have proven vulnerable targets. 
Russia has also stepped up surface fleet and submarine activities in the North Atlantic approaches, the North Sea and the Channel, where it is suspected of mapping underwater infrastructure with a view to future sabotage. Last Monday, one of its warships went a step further , marking Andy Burnham’s first day as UK prime minister with a rare live-fire drill 70kn (45 miles) south of Plymouth, home of the Royal Navy. 
It was the latest in a string of hostile actions designed to provoke, intimidate and test British and European defences. Last month, a Russian frigate fired warning shots near a private yacht off the Isle of Wight. The incident seems trivial until it is set in the wider context of a rapidly building Nato-Russia at-sea confrontation. Then it begins to look scary. skip past newsletter promotion 
after newsletter promotion 
The sense of increasing inter-state maritime lawlessness is fed by numerous other recent incidents, such as the unlawful US sinking of an Iranian warship off Sri Lanka in March, last week’s bitter clash between Chinese and Philippine ships, Trump’s revived threats to forcibly annex the Danish-owned island of Greenland and his bombing of civilian boats off Venezuela. A Chinese nuclear submarine test-fired a long-range ballistic missile in the South Pacific this month to the outrage of Australia, which is itself acquiring nuclear-powered subs . 
US submarine sinks Iranian warship near coast of Sri Lanka – video 
All this instability is fuelling an accelerating global arms race . Little wonder Burnham’s revamped government faces pressure to greatly increase defence spending , especially on the badly depleted Royal Navy. Current UK plans include upgrades to the Trident at-sea nuclear deterrent. 
This many-fronted war of the sea tells a bigger story still: of how centuries-old, hard-won maritime cooperation and collaboration protocols are breaking down, of how international legal norms and rules – whether the issue is free trade, offshore defence, sovereignty, borders, fisheries, deep-sea mining or environmental pollution – are sinking beneath the waves. 
It’s a story about a world where one country can impose its will on others less powerful and less wealthy, rather than seeking their agreement; where the fundamental concept of global commons or shared space is shot to hell. It’s about Lord Palmerston-style gunboat diplomacy writ large. It’s about a world all at sea.

Cars swept away and trees toppled as Typhoon Noul brings flooding to southern China – video 
Typhoon Noul forces more than 715,000 from homes and cancels hundreds of flights in China and Hong Kong
Noul is the strongest typhoon to make landfall in China so far this year, state media reported 
Typhoon Noul made landfall early Sunday bringing strong winds and heavy rain to southern China, including Hong Kong , over the weekend. 
It prompted the evacuation of hundreds of thousands of people in Guangdong province with the region on high alert and hundreds of flights cancelled. 
The typhoon – the strongest to make landfall in China so far this year – will dump heavy to torrential rains across much of southern China for two days, authorities said, after ⁠sweeping the province of ⁠Guangdong ​and neighbouring Hong Kong with gale-force winds. 
China declared its highest alert for flash floods ⁠in several provinces. 
The ⁠year’s 12th tropical cyclone and China’s third this month, Noul, which ​means the glow of sunrise ‌or sunset in Korean, struck ‌the coast of Huidong county about 3.50am, officials ‌said. 
It is expected to bring strong winds and heavy rain to nearby provinces such as Jiangxi and Hunan as it moves inland, state media said, with the rains likely to persist until Tuesday. 
Extremely heavy to exceptional downpours are expected to lash some areas including the ‌province of Fujian, as the National Meteorological Centre forecast heavy to torrential rain from Sunday until Monday morning across ​much of China’s south. 
Authorities urged local governments to pay special attention to flood-prone areas such as zones of mountains and rivers, building sites, valleys and bridges. Weather tracker: More than 900 wildfires rage across Canada 
Read more 
Hong Kong’s Observatory said Noul, with maximum sustained winds of 110 km/h (68 mph) near its centre, was moving Sunday into inland Guangdong and weakening progressively. 
More than 715,000 people had been relocated for safety in Guangdong province, according to state media. Train services in the province were cancelled for Sunday, according to China News Service. 
China’s National Meteorological Center expected parts of southern Guangdong and south-eastern Fujian provinces to experience heavy rain and strong winds. Many trees were seen uprooted in Huilai county, located on the coast of Guangdong province, state broadcaster CCTV reported. 
View image in fullscreen 
People brave the heavy wind and rain as they cross a street in Hong Kong. Photograph: Tyrone Siu/Reuters 
Hong Kong’s airport authority said about 350 flights were cancelled Sunday. At least nine people were injured across the city during the typhoon period, according to authorities. Officials said flights will gradually begin resuming on Sunday afternoon. 
As Noul approached Hong Kong, parts of a large scaffolding on a high-rise building collapsed on Saturday, police said, although initial reports indicated there were no injuries. 
Taiwan’s Central Weather Administration said Noul was bringing rainfall to parts of southern and eastern Taiwan. It was passing over waters south of Taiwan, and was moving away from the island on Saturday. 
This month, Typhoon Bavi brought strong winds and rain to eastern China, leading to the evacuation of more than 2 million people. It made landfall on 11 July. Another, Maysak, made landfall in southern China on 3 July.
